props.title: Tropical Malady
props.initialSlug: A soldier's romance becomes jungle spirit pursuit

sections.content: Tropical Malady (2004) marks a revolutionary shift in Thai cinema, with director Apichatpong Weerasethakul crafting a hypnotic two-part narrative that begins as a tender gay romance before morphing into a mystical folk tale. The film's radical structure influenced later works like Uncle Boonmee Who Can Recall His Past Lives (2010) and Cemetery of Splendor (2015), establishing Weerasethakul's signature blend of reality and myth. Its dreamlike approach to queer desire in rural Thailand opened doors for films like Happy Together (1997) and Call Me By Your Name (2017) to explore LGBTQ+ themes through heightened visual poetry.

movies.slug: Surreal Thai drama about a dying man encountering spirits

sections.content: The film's second half, where a soldier tracks a mythical shape-shifting tiger spirit through dark forests, revolutionized how supernatural elements could be integrated into contemporary narratives. This influenced later works like The Shape of Water (2017) and Border (2018), which similarly blur the line between folklore and modern romance. Weerasethakul's use of extended takes and natural sound creates an immersive atmosphere that later inspired films like Silent Light (2007) and Once Upon a Time in Anatolia (2011). SUBHEAD: Impact on Contemporary Asian Cinema

Weerasethakul's bold formal experimentation in Tropical Malady helped pave the way for other Asian filmmakers to push boundaries. Directors like Tsai Ming-liang with The Wayward Cloud (2005) and Lav Diaz with Evolution of a Filipino Family (2004) similarly embrace extended duration and mythological elements. The film's influence extends to works like Poetry (2010) and The Handmaiden (2016), which share its careful attention to nature and human desire.
